To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Euglossa melanoricha females can assess pairwise relatedness and use this information for social contract; (2) reproductive concessions between related and non-related individuals promote eusocial behavior in Euglossa bees.
the reproductive skew in primitively eucocial bees is strongly associated with genetic relatedness and the social structure of the group.
reproductive concessions between related and non-related members promote eusocaility in primitively euglossine bees.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of eusociality, a major transition in evolution, and how relatedness influences social interactions in small insect societies.
the evolutionary and social consequences of the genetic structure of eusocial associations.
the evolution and maintenance of social behavior in bees, and the mechanisms that regulate the distribution of reproduction among individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the social contract in these bees is based on the genetic relatedness of the partners.
the reproductive concessions between related and non-related individuals are a key factor in the evolution of sociality in Euglossa bees.
reproductive concessions are a mechanism for the maintenance of eusociality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
reproductive concessions between related and nonrelated individuals are a common feature among social insects and may have been important in the evolution of eusociality.
the inclusive fitness theory, as well as the genetic relatedness theory, is supported by our data.

the reproductive concessions between related and nonrelated females in E. melanotricha are a result of the inclusive fitness benefits that each individual can obtain by helping relatives or by controlling reproduction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inclusive fitness benefits of cooperation can be maximized by allowing related and unrelated helpers to reproduce.
relatedness is not the only factor that determines reproductive skew in social insects.
the evolution of sociality in bees may be driven by the ability of dominant females to assess relatedness and to concede reproduction in a context-dependent way.
